sum: SAP's security team had a heavy week, but investors had reasons to look past it. The software maker rolled out 35 new security notes as part of its November Patch Day, nine of which were classified as critical, according to media reports on Thursday. Four of the vulnerabilities carry the maximum CVSS score of 10.0, affecting NetWeaver, Web Dispatcher and Gateway. There were no indications of active exploitation as of the reports.

The Walldorf-based company also published four GitHub security advisories and updated three previously released notes. The disclosure landed in the same stretch that brought a pair of bullish developments on the commercial side.

On Monday, JPMorgan lifted its rating on SAP from "Neutral" to "Overweight" and raised the price target to 275 euros from 175 euros. Analyst Toby Ogg pointed to artificial intelligence moving from pilot projects into productive use in core enterprise systems, along with progress on SAP's own AI offering. He expects rapid amortization of those investments.

A day later, SAP and AstraZeneca announced an expansion of their partnership. The pharmaceutical group intends to move to SAP Cloud ERP Private under RISE with SAP and is evaluating the use of SAP Business AI. According to SAP, the planned migration covers one of the largest SAP system landscapes in the life sciences sector and builds on a relationship spanning 20 years.

Meanwhile, SAP's share repurchase programme continues to run. Through November 6 inclusive, the company had bought back roughly 9.6 million of its own shares, according to a capital market disclosure published Tuesday. Between November 2 and November 6 alone, about 465,000 shares were acquired via Xetra for an aggregate volume of around 95.4 million euros. An earlier interim report on November 3 covered 50,000 shares purchased on XETRA in the final week of October.

Chief Financial Officer Dominik Asam will take the stage at two investor events in the coming weeks. SAP has confirmed his participation in the Morgan Stanley TMT Conference in Barcelona on November 19, 2026, followed by the UBS Global Technology Conference in Scottsdale on December 1, 2026. Both sessions are scheduled as fireside chats and will be webcast.

sum: SAP is giving customers a more detailed view of the environmental footprint of selected cloud services, adding a sustainability angle to the companys cloud expansion story. ERP Leaders reported on Friday, November 13, that users can now see emissions and energy use linked to their own SAP services, with the information based on the servers supporting those products.

The update covers selected offerings including S/4HANA Cloud and Integrated Business Planning. The report cited SAP News Center and said the company still treats its spend-based estimate as the reference for reporting purposes. That distinction matters for investors because a server-based view can provide a more operational measure for individual services, while a spend-based methodology remains the broader reporting framework.

The announcement gives customers another way to assess the environmental profile of their SAP workloads. For SAP, the change supports the wider positioning of its cloud portfolio as enterprise software buyers place more weight on energy consumption, emissions visibility and reporting requirements. The update does not change the companys financial outlook in the source material, but it adds product detail that may influence cloud procurement decisions.

sum: SAP's capital-return programme has now repurchased roughly 9.6 million shares, the Walldorf-based software group disclosed, after picking up about 465,000 of its own stock for some €95.4 million in the latest tranche. The mandatory announcement, published Tuesday, covered purchases made on Xetra between 2 and 6 November and extends a buyback running since late July 2026, during which SAP has spent approximately €1.66 billion on its own equity.

The buying has come at a markedly lower level than in earlier phases. Between April and August 2025, SAP paid an average of €257.60 per share; the stock now trades at €211.50. That gap has not deterred the group, though the economics of further purchases hinge on whether operations can keep generating the cash to fund them.

Analyst sentiment shifted sharply in SAP's favour at the start of the week. JPMorgan upgraded the stock from "Neutral" to "Overweight" and more than doubled its price target, lifting it from €175 to €275. The broker pointed to artificial intelligence pilot projects moving into productive deployment, a shift that raises the importance of integrated core systems. JPMorgan also voiced greater confidence in SAP's margin stability and in the trajectory of cloud orders. According to reports, the upgrade was the trigger behind the share-price advance at the time.

The case for continued buybacks rests on the top line. In the third quarter of 2026, cloud revenue climbed 26% to €6.67 billion, with the short-term cloud backlog up 28% to €24.1 billion. Group revenue for the quarter reached €10.27 billion, while adjusted operating profit rose 18% to €3.03 billion.

Cash generation is the other pillar. SAP expects free cash flow of around €10 billion for the full year, and has guided to a currency-adjusted adjusted operating profit of €11.8 billion to €12.2 billion for 2026. Meeting those targets is what would give the buyback a durable footing — the cloud growth argues in SAP's favour only to the extent that it converts into rising earnings and the anticipated inflows.

Alongside the financial news, SAP and AstraZeneca announced an expansion of a partnership spanning two decades. The pharmaceutical group will migrate to SAP Cloud ERP Private under RISE with SAP and is evaluating the use of SAP Business AI.

SAP Strengthens AI Credentials With Fifth Gartner Leader Nod and JPMorgan Upgrade
sum: SAP has been named a "Leader" by Gartner in both categories of cloud enterprise software for product- and service-oriented businesses — the fifth consecutive time the company has earned the distinction. According to SAP, it has held Leader status continuously since the relevant assessment quadrants were introduced in 2022. The announcements published today relate to the Gartner report dated November 2.

The recognition covers both companies with product-related business processes and service providers, giving SAP external validation of its cloud enterprise software. What ultimately matters for the economic impact is whether customers see enough value in the offered functions to expand their spending.

For service providers, SAP cites the Project Management Assistant, which is designed to cut resource planning time by 30% and rework by 16%. Both figures come from the company and describe the product's intended benefits. For product-oriented businesses, SAP points to the Supply Chain Planning Assistant, which aims to reduce excess and obsolete inventory by 20% and raise order fill rates by 15% — again, company targets.

Beyond individual product promises, SAP already reports broader deployment of its Joule AI assistant, which runs at hundreds of customers according to company statements — usage that goes beyond isolated pilot projects. SAP's own 110,000 employees also use Joule, with the company quantifying productivity gains at 20% in finance, HR and procurement. That internal experience offers a benchmark for potential benefits, provided comparable improvements can be achieved under customer conditions.

Media reports indicate JPMorgan upgraded SAP from "Neutral" to "Overweight" yesterday. The new price target stands at EUR 275, based on December 2028; the bank had previously set EUR 175 for December 2027. Analyst Toby Ogg justified the re-rating with AI projects transitioning into productive use and progress on SAP's own AI offering. The bank also pointed to SAP's data, integration and governance offerings, and raised its earnings estimates for 2026 to 2028 by a low-to-mid single-digit percentage.
On October 28, SAP and NTT announced a planned collaboration on sovereign cloud and SAP Business AI.

sum: SAP shares closed at €209.40 on Friday after surrendering 3.4%, a decline that had nothing to do with the company's own order book and everything to do with the mood surrounding artificial intelligence. The drop came as a worldwide selloff in AI and semiconductor stocks dragged the DAX sharply lower, leaving Europe's largest software maker among the losers on Germany's benchmark index.

The explanations offered across German media converged on the same theme without naming a company-specific trigger. Public broadcaster tagesschau tied the sector-wide selling to doubts over the profitability of heavy AI spending and the prospect of political headwinds for expanding AI infrastructure. Reuters likewise framed uncertainty around AI equities as the backdrop to the global market slide, while dpa-AFX pointed to fears of tighter AI regulation and possible brakes on growth weighing on German stocks. Börse Stuttgart's market report added concerns about the future momentum of AI investment and political resistance to data-center buildouts, describing a worldwide exodus from AI and chip names.

Against that nervous backdrop, SAP has been quietly making the case that it can spend less on AI, not more. Roughly two weeks ago the company said it would swap out several expensive AI models inside its own products for cheaper alternatives. Finance chief Dominik Asam told Reuters the switch should deliver efficiency gains of more than €2 billion over two years — a target that now faces its first real test in a market openly questioning whether anyone can earn a return on AI at all.

On the product front, SAP announced on October 28 a planned collaboration with NTT covering sovereign cloud and SAP Business AI. The initial focus is on sovereign cloud capabilities for regulated industries, with the two partners intending to combine SAP Sovereign Cloud On-Site with infrastructure and operational services managed by NTT. The arrangement spans both sovereign cloud offerings and AI functionality.

A day earlier, at SAP TechEd on October 27, the company rolled out enhancements for developers and AI agents alongside new governance features. The AI capabilities presented at the event touch Joule, the SAP Business AI Platform and SAP Business Data Cloud, according to the company.

SAP's Pipeline Problem: Signed Contracts and Shipped Products Still Await Their Revenue Test
sum: SAP has stacked up a series of announcements that, taken at face value, sketch a widening sovereign cloud and artificial intelligence franchise. The harder question for investors is how much of that stack has actually begun producing business — and how much remains a promise with a date attached.

The most concrete commitment is a contract with the Dutch defence ministry covering development and operation of a sovereign cloud environment in the Netherlands. Operations are slated to start on 1 January 2028. That gap matters: a signed agreement underpins the outlook for the offering, but it does not demonstrate a running business. Shareholders would be wrong to treat the deal as realized earnings.

On the product side, SAP said yesterday that "SAP Incentive Management, Starter Edition" is now available. The company and Cohere have also made Cohere North generally available on the SAP Business AI Platform, aimed at regulated industries among others. Here the availability is already a fact — unlike the NTT cooperation announced on 28 October, in which the two firms merely declared their intention to work together on SAP Sovereign Cloud and SAP Business AI. Their first named area is combining SAP Sovereign Cloud On-Site with NTT-managed infrastructure and operations. That division of labour could hand SAP an additional route to delivery, but an announced intent is not a completed collaboration.

The distinction between shipping a product and generating demand from it runs through every one of these items. A live application creates a supply; only customer adoption turns it into a sturdier argument for growth. The same logic applies to the sovereign cloud portfolio, which SAP says targets regulated sectors. If clients in those industries buy both sovereign cloud and AI applications, the two lines could reinforce each other and give SAP several points of contact with a customer rather than dependence on isolated cloud projects. That is a possible development, not a guaranteed business effect.

What would tip the scale is evidence of repeatability — whether SAP can turn individual sovereign cloud engagements into a broader offering. Progress that shows the shift from partnership intent to practical execution would say more than the raw count of new announcements.

sum: AMD, which recently joined the ranks of trillion-dollar companies, has gained about 126% this year and is poised to add about $58 billion in market value if premarket gains hold. The company's strong outlook highlighted growing momentum in its server processor business, signaling that spending on AI computing was extending beyond Nvidia's accelerators, which dominate the market.

"We see demand across the data-center business, across our CPU business, as well as our data-center AI business," CEO Lisa Su said, adding the company had been preparing for that growth for several years.
Su said on Tuesday that the company expects overall revenue to rise more than 80% in 2027, which is higher than the 77% growth analysts estimate, according to LSEG data.

AMD's product roadmap and expanding software ecosystem position it to capture a meaningful share of the AI market, while strengthening its role as the leading alternative to Nvidia and supporting further gains in server CPUs, said analysts at TD Cowen.
Last week, rival Intel's shares plunged more than 20% after the company reported weak PC demand, fueling concerns about its reliance on the PC market and relatively limited exposure to AI.

Analysts at Morgan Stanley are cautious about assuming current growth in the CPU server business will continue indefinitely amid an industry-wide shortage, but they believe AMD is executing better than competitors and could continue to capture a larger share of the market.

sum: Anthropic, one of the world's leading artificial intelligence companies, on Monday reported a more than 1,100 percent surge in quarterly revenue and nearly $900 billion in spending commitments as it counts down to its Wall Street listing later this month. The filing said the company has committed to spend about $895 billion, mostly on computing power, with $70 billion of that due before September 2027.
The listing comes amid growing nervousness among investors about the huge sums being poured into AI.

Revenue reached $17 billion in the third quarter, up from $1.4 billion a year earlier, though sales growth slowed from previous quarters amid fierce competition from ChatGPT-maker OpenAI and cheaper models, many of them from China.

The company, whose stock market debut is seen as a gauge of how long the AI spending boom lifting the US economy can last, said in an amended filing that its net loss reached $23.3 billion in the July-September period.
The loss stemmed mostly from non-cash accounting charges linked to the company's rising valuation, the filing showed.
Anthropic also posted an operating loss of $567 million in the third quarter as it paid more for short-term computing capacity.

The IPO will be a major test of the market's faith in the AI boom, with the pool of potential investors set to widen as retail traders get their first chance to buy shares directly in a standalone AI giant.

sum: Investing.com -- SAP SE ADRs (NYSE:SAP) rose over 4% in after-hours trading Wednesday after the enterprise software giant delivered third-quarter results that topped Wall Street expectations across key metrics and raised its full-year revenue outlook.

The Germany-based company reported non-IFRS earnings of €1.89 per share on total revenue of €10.27 billion, ahead of analyst estimates pointing to €1.83 per share and €10.10 billion, respectively. Strong demand for enterprise cloud transformations drove a 26% jump in cloud revenue to €6.67 billion, while current cloud backlog expanded 28% to €24.14 billion, reflecting sustained adoption of the company's core software platform.

Against that backdrop, management narrowed its 2026 financial guidance toward the upper bound of previous expectations. SAP now expects full-year cloud revenue to land at the high end of its €25.8 billion to €26.2 billion target range, while maintaining its projection for non-IFRS operating profit between €11.8 billion and €12.2 billion.

sum: SAP pushed out 19 new Security Notes on its September Patch Day, alongside an update to one previously disclosed advisory, addressing 20 vulnerabilities across its product portfolio. A critical kernel gap and a missing-authentication weakness in the NetWeaver Message Server, which could hand attackers system access, round out the most serious findings.

The affected surface is broad: NetWeaver environments, S/4HANA, the Integration Suite, SAPUI5, the ABAP Developer Tools, the NetWeaver Business Client, and Commerce Cloud Search and Navigation all required fixes. For enterprises running SAP systems on-premises or in the cloud, the September cycle translates into fresh patching work — a recurring burden for the software industry at large, but one that lands with particular weight on SAP given the sheer breadth of its customer base. Kernel-level vulnerabilities are especially delicate because they sit deep in the system architecture, and the steady drumbeat of such advisories underscores how large an attack surface SAP's software landscape naturally presents.

After the stock's recent run, the chance-to-risk profile had simply shifted. When a position has already delivered substantial gains, the marginal value of each additional bet diminishes. That is textbook portfolio management, not a verdict on the company's prospects. Yet the market responded the way markets often do — with selling pressure that had little to do with the underlying fundamentals.

sum: The euphoria that swept SAP's stock last week has hit a wall. After a blistering seven-day rally that saw shares climb more than 20%, the German software giant's equity gave back 4.46% on Thursday, settling at €154.98. The pullback comes as investors digest a flurry of analyst revisions and weigh the cost of the company's aggressive artificial intelligence push against its booming cloud business.

The surge that preceded this week's retreat had its roots in second-quarter results released on July 24. Currency-adjusted cloud revenue grew 24%, while the cloud order backlog swelled 27% to €22.9 billion — a figure that handily beat market expectations and set SAP apart from peers struggling to monetize the AI narrative. The performance was enough to propel the stock from deeply oversold territory, with shares gaining 20.14% in a single week.

Yet beneath the headline growth numbers, a more complicated picture emerged. SAP trimmed its full-year operating profit guidance to a range of €11.8 billion to €12.2 billion, down from a previous ceiling of €12.3 billion. The company attributed the revision to dilution from two recent acquisitions: US data platform Dremio, bought in early July, and Freiburg-based AI startup Prior Labs, whose acquisition closed on July 17. SAP plans to invest more than €1 billion in Prior Labs over the next four years, transforming it into a laboratory for structured-data AI — a strategic bet that is weighing on near-term margins.
The operating margin slipped 0.66 percentage points to 27.8%, underscoring the tension between growth and profitability that now defines the SAP investment case.

The market's reassessment played out across a series of analyst notes published this week. Barclays reaffirmed its "Overweight" rating on July 28 but slashed its price target from €255 to €220, explicitly citing margin pressure from the recent M&A spree. Goldman Sachs followed a day later, keeping a "Buy" rating while trimming its target from €230 to €215, though the bank highlighted the robust cloud backlog and strong product pipeline as offsets to short-term margin risk.
JPMorgan struck a more cautious tone, maintaining a "Neutral" stance with a €175 price target and pointing to the second-quarter margin decline despite solid cloud revenues.

According to SAP's second-quarter 2026 earnings report released after the U.S. market close on July 23, cloud revenue grew 24% year-over-year on a constant currency basis to €6.28 billion (approximately $7.1 billion), slightly above the Bloomberg-compiled analyst consensus estimate of €6.26 billion. The performance underscores how enterprise customers are being forced to accelerate their migration to the cloud as the 2027 end-of-regular-support deadline for traditional on-premise software approaches.

The earnings report showed SAP's total second-quarter revenue reached €9.88 billion (approximately $11.24 billion), also surpassing analyst expectations of €9.85 billion. Non-IFRS operating profit on a constant currency basis rose 9% year-over-year to €2.81 billion (approximately $3.2 billion). At quarter-end, SAP's current cloud backlog stood at €22.9 billion (approximately $26.05 billion), up 26% on a constant currency basis.

CEO Christian Klein stated in the earnings release: "This performance is underpinned by our Autonomous Enterprise strategy, with our autonomous suite and Business AI Platform maintaining strong momentum. Customers choose SAP to achieve accurate and compliant AI outcomes built on their most critical business processes and data."
Full-Year Profit Guidance Raised, Reflecting Recent Acquisitions

Based on the second-quarter performance, SAP slightly raised its full-year 2026 adjusted operating profit guidance. The company now expects full-year Non-IFRS operating profit on a constant currency basis to be between €11.9 billion and €12.3 billion (approximately $13.54 billion to approximately $13.99 billion), compared to the previous guidance range of €11.8 billion to €12.2 billion.

The guidance increase primarily reflects the dilutive impact of two acquisitions completed earlier this month. SAP acquired Dremio, a high-performance data lakehouse platform, and Prior Labs, a startup focused on developing an AI architecture called Tabular Foundation Models.

These AI systems can automate complex business tasks with minimal human intervention, prompting investors to question whether the traditional software-as-a-service (SaaS) pricing model, which largely depends on per-user subscriptions, could face pressure over time. If enterprises eventually require fewer software users, subscription growth could slow across the industry.

At the same time, software companies continue to deal with a difficult macroeconomic backdrop. Higher interest rates, persistent inflation and geopolitical uncertainty have made businesses more cautious about technology spending. Many enterprises are taking longer to approve large software purchases, resulting in extended sales cycles across the industry.

Salesforce is naturally exposed to these trends because most of its revenues come from enterprise customers. Slower IT spending could delay new customer wins and reduce expansion opportunities. However, the recent pullback appears to reflect broader market concerns rather than any meaningful deterioration in Salesforce's business.

Salesforce remains the global leader in customer relationship management software, according to Gartner. sum: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has echoed the optimism of global software leaders and pushed back against the fears of a looming “SaaSpocalypse,” telling audiences at Computex that the rise of agentic AI is creating unprecedented opportunities for software firms. Huang addressed concerns that AI agents could disrupt traditional SaaS models, saying: “A lot of people have said, ‘Jensen, AI is coming. Agentic AI is coming. Therefore, all of the software companies are going to go out of business.’ I said it’s exactly the opposite.” For those unaware, Agentic AI refers to systems capable of accomplishing tasks with minimal human intervention, Huang believes that agents will rely more on tools than ever, software companies remain indispensable provided they adapt their products to be usable by AI.

The remarks made by the Nvidia CEO align with that of TCS CEO K. Krithivasan, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff and SAP CEO Christian Klein. All the tech leaders have described this as a transformative era for software firms. Recently, Benioff also dismissed the fears of “Saaspocalypse,” while Klein noted that AI is enhancing enterprise software rather than replacing it. Together, these leaders are pushing back against investor anxiety that has driven down software stocks with Atlassian, Salesforce, and SAP all falling more than 20% since the start of 2026.
Nvidia CEO feels that it's an incredible time for software companies

Huang further emphasized that opportunity lies in retooling software for AI agents: “This is actually an incredible time to be a software company, but the software has to be presented to the agent in a way that the agent can use it.” This reframes AI as a growth driver, not a threat, for companies willing to evolve their offerings.

Recently, Jensen Huang criticised corporate leaders who are attributing layoffs to artificial intelligence. The chief executive of the US-based chipmaking giant called such explanations “lazy” and questioned how companies could justify job cuts using AI before the technology became widely usable in workplaces.
Speaking to Singapore broadcaster CNA in an interview in Taiwan, Huang said many executives were oversimplifying the relationship between AI adoption and workforce reductions.

Stock of the week: SAP - Europe’s Digital Infrastructure Champion
sum: The technological race in the era of the digital economy is most often viewed through the lens of American tech giants. NVIDIA provides computing power, Microsoft and Google develop artificial intelligence models, while Amazon builds global cloud infrastructure. In this picture, Europe often appears more like an observer than an active participant. But that picture is incomplete.

Alongside the entire race for AI, there is a company that builds neither language models nor hyperscale data centers, yet remains one of the most important pillars of the global digital economy. A company without which thousands of the world’s largest organizations simply could not function normally.

SAP is not a typical software company focused on single purpose applications. It provides systems that sit at the very center of how enterprises operate. Its software records everything that matters inside a business: finance, manufacturing, logistics, procurement, HR, and supply chains. It is not a tool sitting “next to the business,” but rather its digital backbone.

That is why SAP is more than just another technology company. In practice, it controls the layer where the digital representation of the real economy is created. And in the age of artificial intelligence, that layer is becoming increasingly valuable.

Because AI, regardless of how advanced it becomes, still depends on data. Not just any data, but structured, reliable, real time operational data generated by actual business processes. This is precisely where SAP occupies a uniquely privileged position.

From a European perspective, this carries another dimension. In a world where most critical digital technologies originated in the United States, SAP remains one of the very few truly global technology players built in Europe and still headquartered there today. As a result, SAP is increasingly discussed not only as an IT company, but also as a strategic asset for the continent itself.
In effect, SAP is no longer viewed as simply another software vendor, but as a piece of economic infrastructure connecting the traditional economy with the emerging AI era.

sum: Today at SAP Sapphire in Orlando, SAP and Amazon Web Services (AWS) announced plans to build SAP Business Data Cloud (SAP BDC) Connect for Amazon Athena, a new offering that will provide bi-directional zero-copy integration between Amazon Athena and SAP Business Data Cloud.

Building on their long-standing partnership, AWS and SAP are making it easier for customers to access mission-critical SAP data products across AWS services, including Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Quick, and Amazon SageMaker. This will allow teams to deliver self-service analytics and build AI agents across all lines of business—without waiting for IT teams to replicate, prepare, and provision SAP data.

“The next era of business will be defined by how well organizations turn intelligence into action at scale,” said Muhammad Alam, member of the Executive Board of SAP SE, SAP Product & Engineering. “By bringing together SAP Business Data Cloud and widely adopted AWS AI and analytics capabilities, customers can unlock the true potential of data and AI.”

Enabled by SAP BDC Connect, the integration delivers near real-time, zero-copy access to semantically rich SAP data products directly through Amazon Athena, keeping data in place, preserving its original business context, and eliminating replication delays. Customers can query and analyze this data immediately, or choose to store and transform it for use across the broader AWS environment. This gives teams a governed, secure environment within AWS to easily build reports, dashboards, and AI agents.

“SAP and AWS share a commitment to helping customers put their most valuable data to work,” said Ruba Borno, vice president of Global Specialists and Partners at AWS. “By combining SAP Business Data Cloud with the AWSsecure, global infrastructure and advanced AI services, organizations can unlock mission-critical SAP data and act on it at the speed and scale their business demands.”

The Botanist’s Assistant, Townsend’s latest publication, centers around Margaret Finch, a six-foot-tall, big-boned, mid-life research assistant to a charismatic botanist at a small university.

Townsend has garnered praise and attention in the literary world, with best selling New York Times author Nina Simon describing the novel as, “‘The Maid’ meets ‘Lessons In Chemistry.’”

sum: Agentic AI is the hottest trend in ERP as vendors race to offer special-purpose AI agents, development tools for building custom agents and new data products expressly designed for AI.

SAP, along with ERP archrival Oracle, is leading this AI push, especially since the debut of generative AI (GenAI) three years ago. Building on earlier machine learning technology, it first added a GenAI copilot called Joule, later augmenting it with the decision-making and autonomy that define agentic AI. It then added Business Data Cloud for the cross-platform data integration AI needs to be effective.

The promise is AI that can anticipate users' needs, communicate with them in their native language and handle many of the tasks that otherwise require tedious data entry and switching between ERP screens.

But building agentic AI that works across SAP and non-SAP systems isn't easy. In this episode of Enterprise Apps Unpacked, Gianluca Simeone, vice president and chief technology and innovation officer at Capgemini, the French multinational IT services firm, shares lessons learned from practical experience, including the design process, development tools and challenges of integrating SAP AI agents as well as orchestrating their behavior.

Based in Milan, Italy, Simeone has more than 20 years of development experience on SAP platforms. He joined Capgemini in 2013 as an SAP enterprise architect and later worked on development teams focusing on major cloud platforms, including AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure. In recent years, his focus has been SAP AI projects.

In one case, Simeone's team reportedly took just three weeks to use Joule Studio to develop custom agents that work across SAP and non-SAP systems to automate the procure-to-pay process of an oil and gas company.

He said multi-agent orchestration, where agents from different vendors and platforms work together, is still under development as the industry works on protocols and standards. For example, Capgemini has a three-way partnership with SAP and Google to use the latter's Agent2Agent Protocol, enabling agents from both vendors to consume data and communicate with each other. They're experimental now but could be offered to Capgemini clients in a few weeks, Simeone said.

How Heartland Dental Is Leveraging SAP for Digital Transformation in Dental Care
sum: What happens when digital transformation meets dental care? Robert “RJ” Jerome, senior vice president and chief digital officer at Heartland Dental, reveals how SAP solutions contributed to the company’s technological journey.

Heartland Dental is the largest dental support organization in the United States, with over 3,000 supported doctors in more than 1,900 supported practices across 39 states and Washington, D.C. But beyond numbers, what sets Heartland apart is its tight knit community and people culture. As Jerome shared, “The first thing I associate with Heartland is community; we’re doctor-led. In our support role, we don’t tell dentists how to practice. Our role is to make their lives easier—enabling dentists to concentrate on patient care.”

Making lives easier is a vision Heartland shares not only for its supported dentists but for its own operations. The company’s digital journey began “backwards” starting in 2018 with SAP Business Technology Platform (SAP BTP), instead of with ERP, to resolve disparate data from all over. Once SAP BTP was established and adopted by the organization, it then began to incorporate SAP Cloud ERP.

What makes this journey truly stand out is how Heartland is using technology to serve people, supported through seamless integration with tools like SAP Concur solutions, embedded AI—such as smart invoice management—and embedded analytics. These features are freeing up time and resources so teams can focus on what matters most: supporting doctors and improving patient care.

The team has rolled out SAP Build Work Zone across its supported practices and is investing in AI tools like Joule to help employees access information faster, automate repetitive tasks, and focus on what really matters—patient care and experiences. Jerome explained, “Just like we take the administrative burden off our supported doctors, SAP takes the tech burden off us, so we can focus on supporting doctors and their teams.”
Heartland’s next big milestone is going live with SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition and taking AI a step further to automation.
Heartland Dental’s story shows that with the strategic adoption of technological innovations, it’s possible to build a future-ready healthcare support organization grounded in people and purpose.

SAP Shares (ETR: SAP) Hit New Low as Selloff Gathers Pace
sum: SAP’s share price (ETR: SAP) plummeted to a new low of €207.55 today, with the decline accelerating as markets digested a mix of disappointing financial results, regulatory scrutiny, and broader industry concerns. The stock is now firmly entrenched in bear market territory, having fallen 25% since June and registering a year-to-date decrease of 12.79%.

The recent downturn is rooted in several key developments. In October 2025, SAP reported third-quarter revenues of €9.08 billion, falling short of the €9.17 billion expected by analysts. While cloud revenue experienced growth, the 22% increase represented the slowest pace since Q4 2023. This slower growth, coupled with cautious full-year cloud revenue projections (€21.6 to €21.9 billion), triggered an initial 2% decline in the share price upon announcement.

Adding to the downward pressure, SAP is currently facing an antitrust investigation by the European Commission. The investigation centers around potential anti-competitive practices related to software support and maintenance. In response, SAP has proposed concessions aimed at facilitating customer transitions to competing software and clarifying its fee structure. The Commission is currently soliciting feedback on these proposed remedies.

The challenges facing SAP have prompted several financial institutions to reassess their outlook on the company. TD Cowen lowered its price target from $350 to $330, maintaining a Buy rating but acknowledging the mixed third-quarter results and the cautious cloud revenue forecast. BMO Capital Markets also reduced its price target, from $307 to $300, citing strong revenue visibility but expressing concerns regarding a potentially weakening macroeconomic environment.

Broader industry headwinds have also contributed to the selloff. In August 2025, European software stocks, including SAP, experienced significant declines amid growing concerns about the potentially disruptive impact of artificial intelligence. SAP’s shares dropped over 6% during this period, marking its largest single-day loss since October 2020.
SAP is also reportedly considering renewing its bid to acquire BlackLine, a Los Angeles-based accounting software firm, for $4.5 billion.

items.t: SAP Shares Physical AI Partnerships & New Robotics Pilots
sum: New collaborations with leading robotics companies and enterprise partners accelerate autonomous operations across manufacturing, logistics, and field services.

Across industries, operational tasks often require real-time judgement and adaptation to constantly changing conditions. Traditional automation falls short here, as physical execution remains disconnected from business logic.

SAP addresses this gap with its Embodied AI initiative, which extends the impact of SAP Business AI into physical operations. By enabling robots to act with business awareness, they can autonomously execute complex tasks while interpreting real-time enterprise context. This allows organizations to adapt more quickly and reliably to dynamic operational environments.

SAP is uniquely positioned to deliver these innovations due to decades of experience building business applications deeply embedded in the processes that power the modern enterprise. This allows SAP to integrate robotics into business functions seamlessly, and in a way no other company can. As a result, autonomous robots operate as an extension of enterprise systems—not as isolated automation—enabling consistent, context-aware execution in dynamic environments.

To explore how embodied AI can support your operations, contact us here. Current capabilities available for productive use or testing span a range of warehouse and operational scenarios, including picking and placing, asset inspection, quality inspection, and safety inspection.

One of the many strategic initiatives Bosch and SAP are working closely is in the area of embodied AI, where Bosch and SAP is collaborating with Aimbo AG to explore how physical AI can transform warehouse automation. In a joint proof of concept, SAP’s embodied AI capabilities and Aimbo’s Industrial Embodied AI deployment middleware enabled Aimbo’s humanoid robot, Anigon, to execute warehouse tasks based on real-time operational context from SAP Extended Warehouse Management (SAP EWM), including delivery data, order priorities, and storage locations.
This initiative combined SAP S/4HANA-driven workflows directly with autonomous robotic execution at a European Bosch facility.
